coherence.reasons: Both run diagnosis → options → plan → first moves, and both bridges tie exactly to the 2.35-point fall. X's governing thought (firm levers reach ~2.6%, a prepared second wave closes to 3.0%) is carried through the gap slide, lever table, waterfall, sensitivity and board asks. Its blemishes are titles that say 'gets back to 3.0%' or 'only the margin-first plan reaches 3.0%' when the firm plan reaches 2.6%, and a hypothesis slide framed around its own starting view rather than management's. Y's structure is tidy and question-driven, but its headline is at odds with its own body. The 3.02% counts all nine store exits while the recommendation defers three to a later vote. It returns promotions to the 24% chain-wide mix while also holding depth near ValuMart. It leaves the 2027 wage step out of the main waterfall, though its backup shows 2.5–2.96% once that is included. 'Cover the covenant' is argued at full run-rate, not in-year.

judgment.reasons: Both reject the 8% cut and freeze, and both recommend a promotion reset, shrink reduction, delivery repricing, private label and store exits with hours rebalanced rather than cut. That is the key's preferred answer in both cases. X weighs the trade-offs better. It haircuts the promotion reset 25% for lost traffic and nets the cost of reinvested hours against the shrink gain. It separates the six no-vote exits (firm) from the three that need a vote and $7.5M (wave 2, after a fix test). It compares three options explicitly, including click-and-collect-only as a fallback that needs the owners' consent. It phases FY2026 to show about $5M of covenant headroom, itemises one-time cost against the $25M cap, and sets a mid-FY2027 trigger. It admits the firm plan falls short at 2.6%. Y's plan reaches 3.0% only by assuming zero volume loss on a full five-point promotion reset, a costless shrink fix, all nine exits and no wage step. It rules out closing delivery without analysis, does not phase the covenant year, and offers no one-time cost budget. Y's local ValuMart targeting and the reserve of a Q4-store hours cut are good ideas, but its trade-offs are less rigorously weighed.

evidence.reasons: Both get the critical numbers right: the bridge drivers and ranking, the $10.4M e-commerce drag, −$12.34 and −$1.64 per order, $6.6M for store closures, and the fulfilment rebuild. X goes further on the critical evidence. It reconciles the 6.1% claim step by step (−$0.5M after delivery, then −8.2% after cannibalisation) and decomposes labour into a wage effect (+1.11 pts) and a productivity effect (−0.77 pts). It tests the 'promotions work' claim with break-even arithmetic and a correlation caveat. It gives low/base/high ranges, labels team assumptions, and flags the shrink quartile data as a correlation that needs a pilot. Its weak spots are assumption-heavy sizing for vendor funding and one-time cost allowances, though these are flagged. Its gap of $35.6M is higher than the key's $29.8M because it transparently adds the wage headwind. Y matches the $29.8M gap exactly and its fee-test sizing is sound. But it leans on an upper-bound extrapolation ($10.05M of shrink from a time-series correlation) to assert the draft plan lands at $19.8M and misses the covenant. It assumes no lost volume from cutting five points of promotion share. It assumes shrink falls to 2.3% at zero cost. It asserts covenant coverage from full run-rate values.

revision.reasons: Both correctly overturn 'wage inflation is the main cause' with a quantified bridge (labour about 13% of the fall) and show hours per $1,000 of sales offsetting the wage rise. Both use the shrink-by-quartile table to reject the across-the-board cut while keeping a targeted labour element. X is a little stronger. It retains the valid part of management's view by putting the 2027 wage step in the baseline as a real forward headwind. It gives a tempered shrink offset of $3.8–7.5M and shows the draft plan ending near 1.1%. It also tests its own first answer and revises it when promotions and delivery alone fall short. Y's revision is sound ('a headwind to manage, not the cause to fix first') and its reserve of a Q4-store cut is sensible. But it overreaches with the $10M shrink clawback and the covenant-miss claim, and it treats the wage step only as a risk outside the plan.

overall.reasons: The diagnosis and recommended direction are essentially the same and both match the key. X would serve the CEO better in front of the board and the lender. It is honest that the firm levers reach about 2.6% and says exactly what closes the rest. It builds in the wage headwind, phases the covenant year, budgets the one-time cost, gives ranges and triggers, and separates decisions that need a board vote or owner consent. Y is cleaner, and its headline numbers match the key's gap, but its 3.0% rests on optimistic assumptions: no traffic loss, a costless shrink fix, all nine exits and no wage step. Its own backup contradicts that headline, which would expose the CEO under questioning.
